newsitem.title: INDIA: India cannot avoid oil price hike, say analysts.
newsitem.headline: India cannot avoid oil price hike, say analysts.

text.p: India cannot avert a fresh hike in petroleum product prices, oil analysts said on Wednesday, reacting to Finance Minister Palaniappan Chidambaram's statement that it would be difficult to raise prices.
"I see them raising prices within one month," an oil analyst at an equities research firm in Bombay said. "One price hike to raise some 50 billion rupees is inevitable," he said.
On Wednesday, Chidambaram told Reuters Financial Television in Tokyo that it would be difficult to raise domestic retail prices of petroleum products.
"The government is considering various options. Just last July we raised petroleum prices, it is difficult for the government to raise prices again," he said.
India's petroleum ministry estimates that oil pool deficit is expected to jump to 155 billion rupees for the year ending on March 31, 1997, against 57 billion rupees a year ago.
The government reimburses oil firms for the difference between what it pays to import crude and what local refiners pay for oil. The oil pool account manages the oil subsidies.
"The deficit should not be less than 135 billion rupees," said another oil analyst, who said the international oil prices had softened after petroleum ministry calculated the figure.
Most analysts expect crude prices to soften further in 1997.
The agreement between the United Nations and Iraq to allow the latter to export oil is also expected to increase supplies.
Delegates at an OPEC oil meet in Vienna on Tuesday were banking on western consumer demand for winter fuel to soak up any resumed Iraqi sales and prevent a big drop in petroleum prices.
"We are looking at a loss of $2.0 in oil prices in 1997," said an analyst. Another oil analyst said he was expecting average Brent prices to slip to $19 in 1997 from current $23 a barrel.
He said India would have to raise its government-fixed prices just once. "Then the deficit may start coming down (reflecting an expected downtrend in global oil prices)."
